msgs.title: The most boring habit in investing is the one that pays.
msgs.pub:
The most boring habit in investing is the one that pays.

Camus wrote about Sisyphus pushing his rock up the hill forever. It rolls down, and he walks back after it.

Camus said we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Rebalancing feels like that. You trim what ran and add to what fell. Next quarter, again.

Retail hates it because nothing exciting ever happens.

The dull push is where the money comes from.

I have learned to like the walk back down the hill.

msgs.title: Every sharp operator becomes the mark one day.
msgs.pub:
Every sharp operator becomes the mark one day.

Daniel Drew spent years as the spider of the Erie pool. He trapped the flies.

Later, his old pupils invited him into a blind pool. Put in millions, close your eyes, trust us.

The game had changed under him. Shorting had stopped working.

His experience felt like an edge. It had become a blind spot.

When someone asks you to put money in and not look, you are the fly.

I only hold positions I can see from top to bottom.

msgs.title: Shorting a market because it feels too high is like ordering the tide back.
msgs.pub:
Shorting a market because it feels too high is like ordering the tide back.

The old English chronicle tells how King Canute set his throne on the shore.

He commanded the sea to stop. The water rose over his feet.

He did it to show his court that even kings have limits.

Perma-bears forget that part. They stand in the surf and shout at the chart.

The tide turns on its own clock, when the buyers run out.

I wait for the water to start going out before I bet against it.

msgs.title: Calling a top too early costs the same as being wrong.
msgs.pub:
Calling a top too early costs the same as being wrong.

In the Greek myth, Apollo gives Cassandra the gift of seeing what comes next.

Then he curses her. Nobody will ever believe her.

She warns Troy about the horse. They pull it inside the walls anyway.

Markets have their own Cassandras. Short sellers who saw the bubble a year before it broke, and blew up first.

The money goes to whoever is still standing when the horse opens.

So I keep my bearish bets small enough to survive being early.

Every model you trust was built on markets that already happened.

You have to use the past. There is nothing else to study.

The future has not been tested yet.

A backtest that never lost in twenty years has never seen next year.

I size every system as if its worst drawdown is still ahead.

It usually is.

msgs.title: The last leg of a panic is rarely about fear.
msgs.pub:
The last leg of a panic is rarely about fear.

It is about margin calls.

Funds that must sell will sell, and brokers sell for retail on margin. Price stops mattering.

Then one morning nobody is left who has to sell.

The bounce starts with no news, and everyone hunts for a reason.

There is none. The forced sellers are simply gone.

That is why the first rally after capitulation feels wrong to buy.

Watch who still has to sell. The headlines come later.

msgs.title: Selling a winner too early hurts more than never owning it.
msgs.pub:
Selling a winner too early hurts more than never owning it.

You can watch a stock you never held run for months with no pain at all.

Sell one you owned, and every new high feels like money taken from your pocket.

The profit you booked stops counting. Only the missing part stays in your head.

That is how late bulls get made. They buy back higher just to stop the itch.

The trades that hurt me most were the ones I chased back.

Take the profit and close the chart.
